project: AI Heritage Revive — Walled City of Lahore
sources: Lahore: A Framework for Urban Conservation (Aga Khan Historic Cities Programme, 2019)
Field photography and GPS capture (personal visit)

landmarks.name: Sheesh Mahal
landmarks.description: One of the most celebrated monuments in Lahore Fort, the Sheesh Mahal (Palace of Mirrors) was built by Shah Jahan as part of the Shah Burj complex. Its facade consists of five multi-cusped marble arches supported by coupled columns. The interior walls and ceilings are encrusted with intricate mirror and coloured-glass mosaic work (kund-kari), reflecting candlelight to create a dazzling effect.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — UNESCO World Heritage Site component

landmarks.name: Naulakha Pavilion
landmarks.description: The Naulakha Pavilion is a small but exquisitely crafted white marble pavilion built by Shah Jahan. Named for its reputed construction cost of nine lakhs of rupees, it features a distinctive curved Bengal-style (bangaldar) roof rarely seen in Lahore Fort. The interior and exterior surfaces are decorated with pietra dura inlay (parchinkari) — coloured stone inlaid in intricate floral and geometric patterns.
landmarks.significance: High — unique bangaldar roof; finest pietra dura work in the Fort

landmarks.name: Picture Wall
landmarks.description: The Picture Wall is a 1,450-foot-long exterior wall running along the northern and western faces of Lahore Fort. Decorated with elaborate glazed-tile mosaic work (kashi-kari) depicting hunting scenes, mythological animals, polo matches, and portraits of courtiers. It is considered one of the largest examples of Mughal decorative tile-work in existence.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — largest Mughal tile-work panel in existence

landmarks.name: Sehdari Pavilion
landmarks.description: The Sehdari Pavilion (Three-Doored Pavilion) is a delicate open pavilion within the Shah Burj complex. Its name refers to its characteristic three-opening facade, a common Mughal architectural motif used to frame views and allow air circulation through the royal apartments. The pavilion served as a pleasure kiosk and viewing platform for the royal family.
landmarks.significance: Medium — elegant example of Mughal open pavilion architecture

landmarks.name: Khwabgah-i-Jahangiri
landmarks.description: The Khwabgah-i-Jahangiri (Sleeping Chamber of Jahangir) was the private bedroom and innermost sanctuary of Emperor Jahangir within Lahore Fort. Located behind the Daulat Khana, it represents the most private zone of the imperial residential complex. The chamber's interior once featured painted plasterwork and carved wooden screens providing ventilation and privacy to the sleeping emperor.
landmarks.significance: High — innermost private imperial apartment; rare surviving sleeping chamber

landmarks.name: Jahangir's Quadrangle
landmarks.description: The largest quadrangle within Lahore Fort, built during the reign of Emperor Jahangir. The courtyard was recently restored with its historical water features and pools reinstated. The four sides of the quadrangle are lined with elegant arcaded halls. The northern facade, known as the Daulat Khana-e-Khaas-o-Aam, is a masterpiece of early Mughal architecture.
landmarks.significance: High — central Mughal residential complex; recently restored

landmarks.name: Sikh Wall
landmarks.description: The Sikh Wall represents the additions and modifications made to Lahore Fort during the Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh. After the decline of the Mughal Empire, the Sikhs took control of Lahore Fort and made significant structural changes, including new fortification walls. This wall section is one of the visible remnants of the Sikh period's architectural interventions.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving Sikh period fortification within the Fort

landmarks.name: Arz Gah
landmarks.description: The Arz Gah (Hall of Petitions) was the formal space within Lahore Fort where petitioners and visiting dignitaries presented their cases and gifts to the Mughal emperor. Located adjacent to the Diwan-i-Aam, it served as an antechamber to the main audience hall.
landmarks.significance: Medium — important administrative space of the Mughal court

landmarks.name: Shah Jahan Quadrangle
landmarks.description: The Shah Jahan Quadrangle is one of the principal open courts within Lahore Fort, developed during the reign of Emperor Shah Jahan. The quadrangle is flanked by arcaded halls and residential chambers that once housed the emperor's private quarters. Shah Jahan's architectural vision — white marble, intricate inlay, and formal garden layouts — is expressed throughout.
landmarks.significance: High — central to Shah Jahan's Fort expansion

landmarks.name: Diwan-i-Khas
landmarks.description: The Diwan-i-Khas (Hall of Private Audience) was the exclusive chamber where the Mughal emperor received high-ranking nobles, foreign ambassadors, and senior ministers in private. Unlike the Diwan-i-Aam which was open to the public, access to the Diwan-i-Khas was strictly limited to the most senior courtiers. The hall featured marble inlay work and intricate carved stone screens.
landmarks.significance: High — imperial private audience hall; restricted access during Mughal period

landmarks.name: Lal Burj
landmarks.description: Lal Burj (Red Tower) is one of the defensive bastions of Lahore Fort, named for its characteristic red brick construction. Located at a corner of the Fort's defensive perimeter, it originally served as a military watchtower and cannon platform. Its red brick construction contrasts with the white marble of Shah Jahan's later additions.
landmarks.significance: Medium — early Mughal defensive architecture

landmarks.name: Kala Burj
landmarks.description: Kala Burj (Black Tower) is a defensive bastion on the northern perimeter of Lahore Fort, paired architecturally with the nearby Lal Burj (Red Tower). Named for its darker stone construction, it served as a watchtower and defensive position. Together, Kala Burj and Lal Burj formed a pair of complementary towers guarding the north-western approaches to the Fort.
landmarks.significance: Medium — paired defensive tower; complements Lal Burj

landmarks.name: Khilwat Khana
landmarks.description: The Khilwat Khana (Private Retreat or Seclusion Chamber) was the emperor's most private space within Lahore Fort — a secluded room used for meditation, private prayer, and moments of personal reflection away from the demands of court. Adjacent to the Shahi Hammam, it formed part of the innermost private zone of the imperial residential complex.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving imperial seclusion space

landmarks.name: Pain Bagh
landmarks.description: Pain Bagh (Lower Garden) was the formal garden of the ladies of the imperial household — the zenana. Located in the southern part of Lahore Fort, it was a private garden space reserved for the royal women. Designed in the Mughal charbagh (four-garden) tradition with water channels, flowerbeds, and shaded walkways, it provided a secluded outdoor space for the imperial harem.
landmarks.significance: High — rare surviving zenana garden within a Mughal fort

landmarks.name: Shahi Hammam
landmarks.description: The Shahi Hammam (Royal Baths) was the imperial bathhouse complex of Lahore Fort. Built during Shah Jahan's reign, it featured a sophisticated system of hot and cold rooms, steam chambers, and underfloor heating (hypocaust) based on the Persian hammam tradition. The walls were decorated with polychrome tile-work and painted plaster. It provided the royal family with bathing and grooming facilities of the highest standard.
landmarks.significance: High — finest surviving Mughal royal bath complex in Lahore Fort

landmarks.name: Athdara
landmarks.description: Athdara (Eight-Columned Pavilion) is an open marble pavilion built by Maharaja Ranjit Singh as his personal court and audience space within Lahore Fort. The name refers to its eight columns supporting the roof. Ranjit Singh held court here, dispensed justice, and received visitors in the open air, following a tradition of accessible kingship. The pavilion is a fine example of Sikh-period architectural refinement blending Mughal marble craftsmanship with Sikh spatial sensibility.
landmarks.significance: High — Maharaja Ranjit Singh's personal court; finest Sikh period structure inside the Fort

landmarks.name: Haveli Mai Jindan
landmarks.description: Haveli Mai Jindan is the residential quarters associated with Rani Jindan, the youngest wife of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and mother of the last Sikh ruler Maharaja Duleep Singh. She served as regent after Ranjit Singh's death in 1839. The haveli represents the Sikh period's residential architectural tradition within the Fort.
landmarks.significance: High — rare Sikh-period residential structure; associated with a major historical figure

landmarks.name: Moti Masjid
landmarks.description: The Moti Masjid (Pearl Mosque) is a small but elegant private mosque built within Lahore Fort for the imperial family's personal prayers. Constructed of white marble, it features three domed bays and a rectangular prayer chamber, notable for its fine proportions and purity of white marble.
landmarks.significance: Medium-High — example of imperial private mosque architecture

landmarks.name: Maktab Khana
landmarks.description: The Maktab Khana (Royal School or Scriptorium) was the imperial space designated for learning, manuscript copying, and royal correspondence. Mughal emperors placed great value on education and literary culture — Jahangir and Shah Jahan both maintained extensive court libraries.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving educational structure within a Mughal fort

landmarks.name: Doulat Khana Khas-o-Aam
landmarks.description: The Doulat Khana Khas-o-Aam (House of Wealth, Private and Public) forms the northern arcade of Jahangir's Quadrangle. It was one of the most important residential and administrative buildings of Lahore Fort, serving as both private imperial apartments and semi-public reception space. The facade is a masterpiece of early Mughal architecture.
landmarks.significance: High — central residential complex of Jahangir's Fort

landmarks.name: Diwan-i-Aam
landmarks.description: The Diwan-i-Aam (Hall of Public Audience) is where the Mughal emperors held open court sessions to hear petitions from ordinary citizens. The structure is a colonnaded hall facing an open quadrangle. A raised marble platform at the rear marks where the imperial throne once stood.
landmarks.significance: High — major Mughal administrative monument

landmarks.name: Shah Burj Gate
landmarks.description: Shah Burj Gate (also known as Hathi Pol or Elephant Gate) is the northern entrance to the Shah Burj complex of Lahore Fort. This gate was the ceremonial entrance used by the imperial family to access their private royal quarters in the Shah Burj. The gate is connected to the Hathi Peer Stairs (elephant ramps) which allowed royal elephants to enter the upper Fort complex.
landmarks.significance: High — royal ceremonial gate; connects to Hathi Peer Stairs

landmarks.name: Barood Khana
landmarks.description: The Barood Khana (Gunpowder House) was the imperial armoury and ammunition depot of Lahore Fort. Its thick-walled, vaulted construction was designed to contain accidental explosions. It stands as evidence of the Fort's dual role as both a royal residence and a military stronghold.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving Mughal military-industrial structure

landmarks.name: Alamgiri Gate
landmarks.description: The main western entrance gate to Lahore Fort, built by Emperor Aurangzeb in 1673. The gate faces the Badshahi Mosque across the Hazuri Bagh. It is flanked by two large semi-circular bastions decorated with white marble and faience tile-work.
landmarks.significance: High — primary Fort entrance, faces Badshahi Mosque
landmarks.status: Open to visitors — main entry point

landmarks.name: Royal Kitchen
landmarks.description: The Royal Kitchen (Shahi Bawarchi Khana) is a large complex of vaulted service buildings that once served the royal household. Notable for massive chimneys, ventilation shafts, and storage chambers. Currently being adapted for reuse as a museum as part of the AKTC/WCLA conservation programme.
landmarks.significance: Medium — rare surviving service complex; being adaptively reused

landmarks.name: Loh Temple
landmarks.description: The Loh Temple (also known as Lav Temple) is associated with Lav (or Loh), the legendary son of Rama, after whom Lahore is traditionally named. Along with the Naag Temple, it represents the pre-Mughal Hindu religious heritage of Lahore Fort's site. These temples are among the oldest structures associated with the Fort's location, predating the Mughal construction by many centuries.
landmarks.significance: Outstanding — pre-Mughal heritage; connects Fort to Lahore's founding mythology

landmarks.name: Masti Gate / Akbari Gate
landmarks.description: The Akbari Gate (also associated with nearby Masti Gate) is the oldest surviving gate of Lahore Fort, built during the reign of Emperor Akbar. It reflects Akbar's early architectural style, blending Timurid Central Asian forms with Indian craftsmanship. It was one of several gates constructed to compartmentalise the Fort's functions.
landmarks.significance: Medium-High — oldest surviving gate in the Fort

landmarks.name: Royal Stables
landmarks.description: The Royal Stables were the imperial facilities for housing the emperor's horses, elephants, and other animals essential to court life and military operations. Now largely in ruins, the stables were once a significant part of the Fort's service infrastructure. The remaining walls and foundations give a sense of the scale at which the Mughal imperial court operated.
landmarks.significance: Low-Medium — historical service infrastructure; largely ruined

landmarks.name: Musamman Burj
landmarks.description: The Musamman Burj (Octagonal Tower) is a prominent bastion of Lahore Fort, rising from the northern perimeter wall. Its octagonal form — unusual in Mughal military architecture — gave it both defensive utility and visual distinction. The tower served as a watchtower and could accommodate artillery for the defence of the Fort's northern face.
landmarks.significance: Medium — distinctive octagonal defensive tower; overlooks Picture Wall

landmarks.name: Hathi Paer Stairs
landmarks.description: Hathi Paer Stairs are the broad, gently inclined ramps built within Lahore Fort to allow war elephants and mounted cavalry to access the upper levels. These wide sloping passages were engineered to bear the enormous weight of royal elephants used in ceremonial processions and military displays.
landmarks.significance: High — unique Mughal military engineering; elephant ramps are rare surviving examples

landmarks.name: Akbari Mahal Kutab Khana
landmarks.description: The Akbari Mahal Kutab Khana was the library and manuscript repository associated with Akbar's palace complex within Lahore Fort. Emperor Akbar, despite being unable to read himself, was a great patron of learning and maintained one of the largest manuscript collections of the Mughal Empire. This building served as the centre of literary and scholarly activity during his reign.
landmarks.significance: Medium — Akbar's personal library; centre of Mughal scholarship

landmarks.name: Haveli Karak Singh
landmarks.description: Haveli Karak Singh was the residential mansion of Karak Singh, the eldest son of Maharaja Ranjit Singh and heir to the Sikh Empire. Built in the Sikh architectural style within Lahore Fort's eastern sector, it represents the residential quarters of the Sikh royal family. Karak Singh briefly succeeded his father as Maharaja in 1839 before dying the same year.
landmarks.significance: Medium — Sikh royal residential mansion; historically significant occupant

landmarks.name: Akbari Hammam
landmarks.description: The Akbari Hammam is the bathhouse complex associated with Emperor Akbar's period of Lahore Fort, predating the more elaborate Shahi Hammam of Shah Jahan's time. Built in the Persian hammam tradition with hot and cold rooms, it served the eastern residential section of the Fort. It is one of the earlier surviving bathing facilities within the Fort.
landmarks.significance: Medium — early Mughal bathhouse; precursor to the Shahi Hammam

landmarks.name: British Jail / Qaidkhana
landmarks.description: The British Jail (Qaidkhana) is a Colonial-period addition to Lahore Fort, built by the British administration after they took control of Punjab in 1849. After the Anglo-Sikh Wars, the British converted parts of Lahore Fort from a royal residence into a military and administrative facility. This jail was used to house political prisoners during the colonial period, adding a layer of colonial history to the Fort's multi-layered story.
landmarks.significance: Medium — Colonial period addition; represents the Fort's post-Mughal history

meta.gps_only_note: Landmarks marked gps_only:true are identified purely by GPS proximity — no CNN model trained on them. They appear in GPS-based identification only.
meta.notes: Coordinates sourced from personal GPS field capture during site visit. For gps_only landmarks, identification fires when user is within 30m of coordinates.
